paragraphs.text: A taxi has just pulled up at the Hauptbahnhof, and the passenger is going to the hotel "Michel". The driver is from the north, so he opens with {{de:Moin}} — and then he does what taxi drivers everywhere do: he talks about the city while he drives.

Read it once for the story, then once more with the map on the textbook page in mind. Every place the driver names is a noun with its article attached — {{de:der Bahnhof}}, {{de:die Kunsthalle}}, {{de:das Rathaus}} — because in German a place name on its own always arrives wearing its article.
Der Taxifahrer redet gern. Er zeigt die Orte: der Bahnhof, die Kunsthalle, die Alster, das Rathaus, die Michaeliskirche. Am Ende ist das Hotel schon da.

turns.speaker: Gast
turns.english: Good day. To the hotel "Michel", please.

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.german: Moin. Hotel »Michel«, okay. Kennen Sie Hamburg?
turns.english: Moin. Hotel "Michel", okay. Do you know Hamburg?

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.english: Well then, that's the main train station.

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.german: Und das hier rechts ist die Kunsthalle. Das ist ein Museum.
turns.english: And here on the right is the art gallery. That's a museum.

turns.speaker: Gast
turns.german: Interessant. Und wie heißt der See?
turns.english: Interesting. And what is the lake called?

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.german: See? Das ist kein See, das ist ein Fluss. Der Fluss heißt Alster.
turns.english: Lake? That's not a lake, that's a river. The river is called the Alster.

turns.speaker: Gast
turns.german: Ach so. Und was ist das? Ist das eine Kirche?
turns.english: I see. And what is that? Is that a church?

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.german: Hier ist eine Kirche. Das ist die Michaeliskirche. Wir sagen »der Michel«.
turns.english: Here is a church. That's St Michael's. We call it "der Michel".

turns.speaker: Taxifahrer
turns.german: Und da ist auch schon das Hotel.

paragraphs.text: Grüßen means to greet, and the three German-speaking countries each greet differently in everyday life. In the north of Germany you hear {{de:Moin!}} all day long — it works for good morning and good evening alike, which is presumably why the taxi driver uses it. Austria answers with {{de:Grüß Gott!}}, Switzerland with {{de:Grüezi!}}.

{{de:Guten Tag}} stays safe everywhere, so it is the form to reach for when you are travelling. The regional ones are worth recognising even if you never say them yourself — and saying {{de:Moin}} in Hamburg will earn you a small nod.
Moin! · Grüß Gott! · Grüezi! · Guten Tag!
